title: Global Error Types Coupling Unrelated Subsystems
pattern: Unrelated modules use one centralized catch-all error enum or class that lists subsystem-specific failures, making local interfaces depend on the entire application's error vocabulary.
why_bad: Local changes propagate through a central dependency: adding a variant for one low-level module edits the global error file and can broaden rebuild and change impact across every unrelated importer. It also prevents local reasoning, as a helper's signature appears to permit unrelated failures such as network errors from pure validation. [24, Chapter 3, "The Error.java Dependency Magnet"]
detection: Breadth case: a massive application error enum, with more than 20 variants across disjoint subsystems (such as databases, third-party APIs, and parsing libraries) as a source heuristic. Dependency case: an error enum or class imported by five or more logically unrelated modules while many variants belong only to one subsystem. Either case suffices; confirm that the type is a shared internal contract, not merely an adapter at final integration.
counterexample: `Context-dependent`. A binary's root error adapter that exists solely to aggregate or map disparate module errors for final logging at the program boundary. A small, highly cohesive utility library with one core purpose may reasonably use one error type.
source: *Robert C. Martin - Clean Architecture (2017)*, Chapter 10; *Steve McConnell - Code Complete (2004)*, Chapter 7; *Robert C. Martin - Clean Code*, Chapter 3, "The Error.java Dependency Magnet" [24]
